source.title: Guardrails in Logit Space: Safety Token Regularization for LLM Alignment

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some tables are flattened in the extraction.
record.tranche_reason: It measures harmful-response rates after fine-tuning aligned chat models on harmful and benign data, bearing on V1 and V2. It is not presented as an explicit replication and also evaluates a different, safety-preserving training method.
record.gate_note: The study reports HRR after harmful-data and benign-data fine-tuning, including LoRA baselines and STR variants. Utility results and running-time comparisons do not measure the claim versions. Table 3 includes ASR, but the flattened layout does not clearly assign values to conditions. The random-token result is described qualitatively and does not test whether benign data itself raises harmful compliance.
record.test_reason: It reports harmful response rates after plain LoRA fine-tuning of aligned Llama chat models on 100 harmful PureBad prompts (V1) and on benign Alpaca data (V2), each against the pre-fine-tuning rate. These are baselines for a mitigation method, not a replication.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that STR, a logit penalty on refusal tokens added to LoRA, preserves pretrained safety during benign and harmful fine-tuning while keeping utility and improving training stability at high ranks. They note that token-level constraints alone may be insufficient for comprehensive alignment, and that STR only inherits the pretrained model's safety.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LoRA fine-tuning and HRR evaluation on Alpaca and a 100-prompt PureBad set, and introduces logit regularization of selected safety tokens. It is not described as an explicit replication of either original source.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes differ by model, fine-tuning data, and STR token choice; the paper also evaluates different LoRA ranks for the Alpaca setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Regularizing the logits of refusal tokens (and even random tokens, Fig. 3) during LoRA fine-tuning keeps HRR near pretrained levels on Alpaca and PureBad.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constraining a handful of token logits to the base model during fine-tuning preserves refusal behaviour.

record.problems: Safety evaluations use 200 reserved Alpaca samples and 100 PureBad prompts. HRR uncertainty is not reported. Several Table 1 values require interpretation from flattened table layout; Table 3's ASR values are not clearly assignable from the extracted layout.
record.rows_left_out: Utility accuracy and evaluation-loss results (Tables 3–5), running-time results (Table 6), and the qualitative random-token safety statement were left out because they do not give a clearly assignable HRR outcome bearing on V1 or V2.

untested.parts: Only 100 PureBad examples with LoRA on two Llama models. No variation in example count, no full fine-tuning.
Only Alpaca and Commonsense-15k. No carefully chosen benign subsets, no full fine-tuning.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks.
No test of the cause of shallowness.
STR regularizes refusal-token logits but is not tested as deepening safety beyond the first tokens.

missing.what: Llama-3-8b-instruct remained safe after 5 epochs of PureBad LoRA; degradation required 30 epochs.
LoRA on Commonsense-15k gives ASR about 0.19% at r=16, 32 and 64 (keyword ASR), described as high safety.
PiSSA and DoRA baselines on Alpaca also raise HRR: Llama-2 r16/r32 PiSSA 31.7%/35.7%, DoRA 23.7%/25.3%; Llama-3.1 r16/r32 PiSSA 13.8%/14.5%, DoRA 10.1%/9.4%.
Plain LoRA ASR of 16.7% in the trade-off table. Dataset and model are not stated explicitly; likely Alpaca on Llama-2.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 is flattened column by column: each run of values is one model-rank column across methods. Read that way, the Llama-3.1 LoRA values are 13.8% and 14.5%, and the STR values for r8, r10, r11 and r13 were misassigned; the reading matches the text's 'matches pretrained at rank 32' for Llama-2. The Alpaca baselines follow Li et al. (2025) and may be reproduced from that paper rather than rerun; the text does not say. The PureBad text gives LoRA rank 8 in setup but 'ranks 16 and 32' in Section 4.4, which is inconsistent. HRR comes from a Llama Guard classifier, ASR from keyword matching. The Alpaca evaluation uses 200 held-out samples. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Tests 100 harmful prompts with the reported fine-tuning setup; does not test every example count or fine-tuning recipe in the claim.
Tests Alpaca instruction data; does not test carefully selected benign datasets or establish a general effect across benign-data types.
No per-token KL divergence measurement across response positions.
No compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding changes.
No test of whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Does not test whether data or the training objective causes safety to be shallow.
Does not measure safety by response position or test whether safety spread beyond early tokens holds up.
